newsitem.title: INDIA: ANZ Grindlays wins $240 million award in India.
newsitem.headline: ANZ Grindlays wins $240 million award in India.

text.p: ANZ Grindlays Bank was awarded substantial compensation that could total $240 million in a dispute with a wholly-owned subsidiary of India's central bank, a senior bank official said on Sunday.

The award, made by an arbitration panel, comprises money forfeited in the wake of a share scandal that rocked India's stock markets in 1992 and is linked to transactions involving Harshad Mehta, a broker nicknamed "the Big Bull" for his role in the scam.

The dispute stemmed from efforts by the National Housing Bank (NHB), a subsidiary of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to recover money paid by cheques, crossed 'account payee only', written in favour of ANZ Grindlays.
ANZ Grindlays, part of Australia and New Zealand Banking Group, maintained that Mehta gave instructions that these cheques should be paid into his personal account.
NHB maintained that this amounted to wrongful collection of the cheques by ANZ Grindlays.
ANZ Grindlays disputed this, saying the cheques represented principal-to-principal transactions between NHB and Mehta.
Subsequently the RBI intervened, directing ANZ Grindlays to pay the disputed 5,065.4 million rupees ($141 million) to NHB.

The arbitration panel, which met in a Bombay hotel on Saturday, ordered that the money be repaid to ANZ Grindlays together with interest dating from 1992 -- which newspapers estimated at around four billion rupees.

"The claim of NHB against Grindlays has been dismissed and it has been asked to repay the disputed amount. We will have to wait for the implementation of the arbitration panel's order," Mehli M. Mistri, chief executive officer of ANZ Grindlays in India told Reuters.
Mistri could not confirm the exact interest component, but said the newspapers' estimates were fairly reliable.

"ANZ regards the process under which this dispute was arbitrated as a very positive demonstration of how the business infrastructure in India can cope with major disputes and provide proper resolution of them," ANZ spokesman Rob Gerrand said in a statement issued in Sydney on Sunday.
But the fight is likely to be continued in the courts, Indian newspapers said.

The NHB, backed by the RBI, is likely to challenge the panel's decision, first through a special court set up to investigate transactions related to the five-year-old share scam and later the Supreme Court, the Financial Express said.

The State Bank of India (SBI) said it was encouraged by the ruling in favour of ANZ Grindlays, as it was trying to recover 7.77 billion rupees (excluding interest) it had to pay NHB under pressure from RBI.

"As things stand, the panel's decision is a favourable development for us at SBI and holds promise for us as we can also hope to recover the money we had paid to NHB," M.S. Verma, SBI's managing director told Reuters.
SBI, the country's largest commercial bank, also part-owned by the central bank, did not take the issue to arbitration but sought redemption through court action.

S. Venkitaramanan, the former RBI governor who headed the central bank at the time of the share scandal, said he had no comment to make on the panel's findings but said it could have ramifications for the banking system.

"The RBI as well as the government will have to look at this matter carefully as this has implications for the banking industry as a whole and for the system of collections and payments," Venkitaramanan told Reuters from Madras.

C. Rangarajan, the current RBI governor, said he had no comment to make either, but the Financial Express said Rangajaran held an emergency meeting with NHB officials immediately after the panel announced its decision.

"There is no question of NHB being liquidated. Even if it has to pay up the Reserve Bank has enough profit to recapitalise its wholly owned subsidiary,"the newspaper quoted an RBI official as saying after the meeting. ($1 = 35.90 rupees)
